diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Analysis

The score has stayed at 3.1222 across three structurally different rewrites, and each produced the same cost of 3567. Changing the control-flow layout alone doesn't seem to move the metric, so the remaining lever is the number of SSA instructions executed per word in the hot 16-word path.

In the current code, each `xs[k]` in the 16-word peel is a separate indexed access with its own bounds check. If the interpreter does not eliminate those checks, that's roughly 16 extra compare-and-branch sequences per block. Re-slicing once with `w := xs[:16:16]` gives the compiler a slice whose length is a known constant of 16, so every `w[k]` with constant `k` needs only one length check, performed when `w` is created. The recursion and the tail logic stay the same, so correctness is unaffected.

This is a targeted change that keeps the rest of the program intact. The gain is uncertain, since I can't see whether giri already removes these checks, but it's the most plausible way to cut instructions without changing behavior.
